transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?

Well, I suppose I’m here because... well, it’s work. I drive, you see, I’m in transportation, and lately things have been... complicated. I mean, dispatch and compliance, they're supposed to just monitor the schedules, right? Make sure the routes are covered, log the hours, the usual administrative stuff. But it’s gone way beyond that. They’ve been tracking my specific route changes through the computer system—not just logging them, but *tracking* them. And it’s not just the computer, it’s on the radio too. I hear these little comments, these tiny, specific remarks over the dispatch radio that seem random to anyone else, but I know they’re about me. I know exactly what they’re doing. And I’ve tried talking to a couple of people about it, you know, just testing the waters, and they always say the same thing. They say, "Oh, it’s just normal oversight, they do that to everyone, it’s just compliance checking the logs." But it’s not. I can tell. I can absolutely tell that certain other drivers—drivers I thought I was okay with—are actually reporting on me. They’re feeding information back to dispatch about every little thing I do. It’s like this whole coordinated effort just focused on my vehicle and my shifts, and it’s just... it’s a lot to deal with every single day when I’m just trying to do my job.
How long have you been noticing this coordinated effort against you going on?

Well, if I really sit down and try to trace it back to the exact beginning... it’s been about two months where it’s been absolutely undeniable. Like, crystal clear to me. I mean, before that, maybe there were little things, you know? A weird look in the breakroom or a shift assignment that felt a bit off, but the actual, undeniable tracking? The stuff with the computer system in the cab and those specific, pointed remarks over the dispatch radio? That’s been going on for a solid two months. 

I remember specifically because it was right around the time they updated the routing software, and I was driving the northern corridor a lot more. At first, I tried to rationalize it. I told myself, okay, maybe it's just the new software, maybe dispatch is just being extra careful because of the new update and they're just keeping a closer eye on the metrics. But then the radio clicks would happen exactly—and I mean exactly—when I would take an exit or pause at a weigh station, and they'd say these things... these little coded remarks that perfectly matched what I was doing right at that second. 

I even started marking it down on my calendar at home, just to be sure I wasn't, you know, overthinking it or reading too much into a coincidence. But you can't have coincidences every single day for eight weeks straight. It's been two whole months of this constant, heavy surveillance, every single shift. And it's just exhausting, honestly, trying to keep my eyes on the road and do my job safely when I know that console is basically a homing beacon for them to monitor and talk about me. So, yes, two months of this... this whole ordeal.
Outside of the comments on the radio, have you heard any voices or sounds that others around you cannot hear?

No, no, nothing like that. It's just the radio. I mean, I'm not... I'm not hearing things that aren't there, if that's what you're asking. I know what a hallucination is, and it's not that. The sounds I hear are real. The radio clicks, the static, the actual voices of the dispatchers coming through the speaker—it's all coming from the equipment in the cab. Anyone sitting next to me would hear the exact same audio. The difference is, they wouldn't understand the context. They wouldn't know that when Dispatcher Dave says, "Checking the load balance on the northbound," right as I'm adjusting my seat, he's actually commenting on me. But the voice itself? The sound waves? Completely real. I don't hear whispering in the wind or voices coming from the vents or anything like that. It's all strictly through the communication channels they've set up to monitor us. I'm very grounded in reality when it comes to what I'm hearing physically. It's just... it's the meaning behind it, the constant stream of it through the radio that's the issue. So, no, no voices in my head or anything, just the very real voices of the people tracking me.
Aside from the stress this has caused, have you been feeling persistently down, depressed, or hopeless?

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I'm not sad. Don't get me wrong, the stress is very real, like I was saying. It's incredibly draining to be on high alert for a ten or twelve-hour shift. You get home and your shoulders are just in absolute knots from tensing up every single time the radio crackles. But being exhausted from stress isn't the same as being depressed, you know? 

I still get up every morning right when my alarm goes off. I still make my coffee—I have this whole routine, I use a French press every single day because you really need a strong, dark roast for those early northern routes—and I still care about doing a good job. I'm not sitting around crying in the dark or feeling like there's no hope for my future. My life itself is fine! It's just this one, specific, massive problem at work that's wearing me thin. 

If dispatch would just back off and go back to normal logging, if they'd just stop this whole coordinated tracking thing, I'd be completely fine. It's really just frustration more than anything else. It's so frustrating when you know you have a clean driving record and you're doing everything right, but you're being scrutinized like a... like a test subject or something. Anyone in my shoes, sitting in that cab dealing with those little coded remarks all day, would be stressed out. You'd have to be a robot not to be on edge. But hopeless? No, definitely not. I'm not depressed, I just want them to stop playing these games so I can just do my job and drive in peace.
Have you been diagnosed with any physical health problems or medical conditions?

Physical health problems? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my physical health is actually pretty great, all things considered. I try to take good care of myself because, you know, driving a truck for a living, you really have to. It's so easy to just sit there for hours on end, eating junk food from truck stops—which, believe me, is tempting when you're exhausted and there's a roller grill right by the register—but I don't do that. I actually pack my own meals. I have this little cooler that plugs into the 12-volt outlet in the cab, and I bring salads, some grilled chicken, maybe some fruit... things that won't make me feel sluggish on the road. 

And my DOT physicals? Always perfect. The medical examiner always comments on how good my blood pressure is, which is honestly a miracle given all the stress with dispatch lately. But yeah, no diabetes, no heart issues, no asthma, nothing like that. I don't even get headaches very often, unless I've been clenching my jaw too much from listening to the radio, but that's just tension, not a medical condition. 

I really pride myself on being healthy and capable. You have to be, to handle an 18-wheeler. It takes a lot of physical stamina, even if people think you're just sitting down all day. You're constantly scanning, steering, dealing with the vibration of the road... it takes a toll if you aren't in good shape. So, I make sure I am. I even do some stretches around the rig when I stop for my mandatory breaks. Just, you know, reaching up, touching my toes, walking a lap or two around the trailer to get the blood flowing. So physically, I'm completely fine. It's just... like I said, it's just the situation with the tracking that's the problem, not my body. My body is totally healthy.
Have you ever felt like your thoughts or actions are being controlled or manipulated by an outside force?

Controlled? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I'm the one behind the wheel, right? I'm the one driving the truck. When I put my hands on that steering wheel—and it's a big wheel, you really have to grip it, especially when you're dealing with crosswinds on the interstate out by the gorge—when I turn it, it's my arms doing the turning. My brain tells my arms to move, and they move. Nobody is... making me do anything. I don't feel like a puppet on strings or anything sci-fi like that. 

My thoughts are completely my own, too. I'm just sitting there, thinking about what I'm going to have for dinner, or calculating my remaining hours of service, or, you know, just focusing on the road ahead. The dispatchers, the people on the radio I was telling you about? They're observing me. They're watching and they're making their little comments, sure, but they aren't forcing me to act. Like, if I reach over to adjust the AC because it gets really stuffy in the cab around mid-afternoon when the sun hits the windshield directly, and then the radio clicks and they make a remark about the "temperature rising"—they're just reacting to what *I* chose to do. They didn't make me reach for the dial. I have complete free will. 

I think if someone was actually trying to control my actions, I wouldn't be able to do my job at all. You can't drive an 80,000-pound vehicle if you aren't 100% in charge of your own reflexes. You have to be sharp. You have to anticipate traffic, watch out for the four-wheelers who just zip in and cut you off because they don't understand braking distance... I make all those split-second decisions myself. I have to. So no, my thoughts and my actions are completely mine. It's just the surveillance that's the issue, the constant monitoring, not any kind of... mind control or whatever. I'm entirely my own person.
